newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha to get fresh term as anger grows.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha to get fresh term as anger grows.

text.p: Albania's ruling Democratic Party was poised on Thursday to choose President Sali Berisha for a second term in office while student-led protests grew over the government's handling of a pyramid investment scandal.
The Democrats' 105-member executive national council met in Tirana to select Berisha as their candidate in a parliamentary vote next week to elect a new president.

"Berisha is the most complete democratic and national figure who can establish dialogue, justice and equilibrium in the country to secure its development and integration in Europe," a statement from the party said.
The main opposition Socialist Party has refused to take up its seats in parliament after boycotting last May's general election, alleging the Democrats manipulated the vote.
Their leader Fatos Nano, the only serious rival to Berisha, is in jail for corruption. But the Socialists say he is being held on trumped-up charges and is a political prisoner
Berisha won office in 1992 as the charismatic leader of a Democratic Party which swept the Socialists, the former communists, from power in a landslide general election victory.

But Berisha, a former communist and heart surgeon, and his right-wing party are faced with their biggest crisis following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes which has left thousands of Europe's poorest citizens out of pocket.

While Democrats met in the Palace of Congresses in central Tirana, around 700 students gathered at a Tirana university building some 500 metres (yards) away to voice their support for students on hunger strike in the southern town of Vlore.
"If we do not have an answer by noon we shall escalate our protest and go on hunger strike ourselves," a student leader said. "Only the president can solve the problem."

Police and security forces have used heavy-handed tactics to prevent students in Tirana from staging demonstrations. High school pupils announced they would stay away from classes but police officers forced them into school buildings on Thursday.

Student protests have a symbolic significance in Albania because students were a driving force in demonstrations that toppled the 45-year Stalinist regime in 1990, forcing then communist president Ramiz Alia to permit multi-party democracy.
Students were also behind the founding of the Berisha's own Democratic Party.
In Vlore, 140 km (90 miles) south of Tirana, protesters were out on the streets for the 22nd consecutive day in a peaceful demonstration against the investment scandal.
Violent clashes hit Vlore two weeks ago when one man was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks.

Thousands poured into the streets on Wednesday evening after rumours that riot police were on their way to evict around 45 students who began their second week on hunger strike, and who have become a fresh focus of anti-government resentment.

No police arrived but that did not stop villagers from the Vlore area expressing their support for the town on Thursday, marching peacefully in the streets, carrying axes and scythes. Small rightist opposition parties in parliament said they would not select their own candidate for the presidency and Berisha was likely to enter the election unopposed.
"There's no point presenting a candidate in a parliament dominated almost 90 percent by the ruling party," Republican Party leader Sabri Godo told Reuters.
